rationale: The BOOK ENTRY's core — scarlet as covenant blood displayed outwardly — is carried better by the four printed texts than the strongest rival (scarlet = sin's stain). Hebrews 9:19 places scarlet wool literally in the hand that sprinkles 'the blood of the covenant' on book and people: covenant blood applied outwardly, in public view. Joshua 2:18 is a scarlet line displayed in a window as the visible token that spares a household — blood-sign displayed outwardly, not sin. The sin-only reading has no non-strained account of either passage; scarlet in the tabernacle/purification stream and in Rahab's cord is salvific and ritual, not culpable. Isaiah 1:18 is the sin-reading's anchor, but it does not defeat the book: sins 'as scarlet' in context of Isaiah 1:15 ('your hands are full of blood') are blood-guilt worn visibly, and the same oracle commands washing white — the stain and the cleansing are both blood-colored, which the book's covenant-blood identification absorbs (the chapter's Rev 7:14 parallel: robes made white in the blood of the Lamb). The entry's one printed secondary assertion — the color counterfeited by those wearing form without substance — is directly evidenced by Revelation 17:4, where the harlot is arrayed in scarlet outwardly while her cup is full of abominations: the covenant color worn without the covenant. The blood/atonement alternative acknowledged as 'common' in every common-interpretation response shares the book's core referent, and under the rules a counter that agrees with the core referent yields PERSUADED. No supplied text is explained by the sin-reading that the book's core cannot explain without contradiction.
book_core_identification: Scarlet symbolizes covenant blood made outwardly visible — the blood of the covenant displayed as a sign (sprinkled with scarlet wool, hung as a scarlet line) — with the corollary that the color can be worn falsely by those who display the form without the covenant substance.
book_secondary_elaborations: The scarlet sign is counterfeited: some wear the covenant color outwardly without its substance (Rev 17:4, the harlot arrayed in scarlet with a cup of abominations).
chapter_only_objections: The supporting chapter (Garments & Armor) treats garments, nakedness, and armor broadly and gives scarlet itself only indirect treatment (Isa 1:16-18 within the robe-washing argument); the entry's specific derivation of scarlet rests more on the four printed references than on the chapter.
The chapter's claim that KJV 'righteousness of saints' obscures dikaiōmata and that this built 'a long confusion' is a doctrinal-polemical claim beyond the glossary term.
The chapter's identifications of the bath as baptism, feet as walk/conduct, and the helmet of yeshuah as Christ covering the mind are separate symbol claims not asserted by the scarlet entry.
The fig-leaf/false-covering typology and the Saul-armor 'assay' reading are chapter-level applications outside the scarlet entry's scope.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Scarlet primarily symbolizes sin — deep-dyed, conspicuous, seemingly permanent guilt that can nonetheless be cleansed white — with Isaiah 1:18 as the anchor text and Revelation 17-18 reinforcing scarlet's negative association with corruption and immorality.
counter_core_identification: Scarlet = the ingrained stain of sin and guilt.
material_core_denial: If scarlet's fixed symbol is sin, then scarlet is not covenant blood displayed outwardly; the two identifications assign opposite valences (culpable stain vs. saving sign) to the same color and cannot both be the core referent.
counter_case: Isaiah 1:18 explicitly equates sins with scarlet/crimson, the most famous scarlet text in Christian usage.
Revelation 17:4 dresses the abomination-filled harlot in scarlet, reinforcing a negative, sin-linked valence.
Homiletic and popular tradition (hymns, sermons) has made 'sin as scarlet' the reflexive association, as all four common-interpretation responses attest.
book_explanatory_advantages: Hebrews 9:19 directly binds scarlet wool to the sprinkling of 'the blood of the covenant' — covenant blood applied outwardly; the sin-reading cannot explain why scarlet is the applicator of cleansing blood rather than the thing cleansed.
Joshua 2:18 makes scarlet a displayed saving sign in a window that marks a household for deliverance — display of protective blood-sign, inexplicable as a symbol of guilt.

The entry unifies the positive uses (Josh 2:18; Heb 9:19) and the negative use (Rev 17:4) under one mechanism: genuine display versus counterfeit display of the covenant color — the harlot wears the form without the substance.

Isaiah 1:18 remains explicable: in context (Isa 1:15, hands 'full of blood') sins as scarlet are blood-guilt visibly worn, and the promised whitening matches the book's wash-the-garment pattern (Rev 7:14: robes made white in the blood of the Lamb).
Even the common-interpretation responses concede a 'common' blood/sacrifice/atonement meaning (Rahab's cord as type of Christ's blood, back to 1 Clement 12), which shares the book's core referent.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Isaiah 1:18 is more immediately natural under the sin-reading: the verse itself says 'your sins be as scarlet.'
The sin-reading matches the dominant reflexive association in Christian teaching and requires no typological step at Joshua 2:18.
decisive_sources: Hebrews 9:19 — scarlet wool as the instrument sprinkling the blood of the covenant on book and people
Joshua 2:18 — the scarlet line displayed outwardly in the window as the saving sign
Revelation 17:4 — scarlet worn by the harlot whose cup is full of abominations, the form without the substance
Isaiah 1:15-18 — blood-guilt as scarlet, washed white, consistent with the covenant-blood/washing pattern
unresolved_objections: Isaiah 1:18 reads more naturally on its face as sin-symbolism, and the book's blood-guilt harmonization, while contextually defensible via Isaiah 1:15, is an interpretive step the verse does not state.
The 'covenant' qualifier rests chiefly on one explicit text (Heb 9:19/9:20); Joshua 2:18 supplies it only typologically.
